detail.overview:
Physics doesn't care if your code compiles. It is relatively easy for a language model to ace a textbook thermodynamics quiz or write a self-contained Python script. Designing a real building is a different sport. Try routing chilled-water piping across seven drawing sheets around an offset structural grid and 104 sprinkler heads without putting a steel beam through an air duct.

Most AI benchmarks treat engineering like a trivia night. Models score above 90% on isolated question-answering sets, yet stall out when handed a real project folder. Actual physical engineering isn't a single formula look-up; it is a multi-hour investigation across dozens of messy, interdependent files. Before a school, hospital, semiconductor fab, or data center breaks ground, practicing engineers spend months cross-checking 3D computer-aided design (CAD) geometries, geotechnical soil borings, municipal utility rules, and 50-file specification packages to issue deliverables a licensed reviewer will stamp. Current agents often misread drawing callouts, apply the wrong code clause, drop unit conversions, or quit early—leaving top frontier models scoring below 50%.

Google Cloud AI Research, in partnership with Mercor and alongside academic partners from Stanford, NYU, the University of Washington, UNC Chapel Hill, Harvard, and Columbia, is opening the vault with Physical-Engineering's Last Exam (PLE). For the first time, this release introduces a benchmark of 85 expert-reviewed, long-horizon engineering tasks across four core disciplines: structural, civil, electrical, and mechanical engineering.

In this competition, your task is to build an open-source agent harness, pair it with a Google-sponsored foundation model, and document your engineering findings in a Kaggle Writeup. Instead of wrapping a single prompt around a chatbot, you will engineer the verification loops, CAD and spreadsheet tool integrations, context-management strategies, and self-checks needed to turn raw project folders into graded engineering artifacts—from seismic shear-wall calculations and clay footing settlement memos to clash-free 3D building models in Industry Foundation Classes (IFC4) format and 25-year cooling-tower cost studies.

If successful, your work will help take months of tedious planning overhead off the plates of human engineers and compress infrastructure design cycles down to days.
detail.evaluation:
Submissions are evaluated in two stages: a 100-point Kaggle Writeup and pre-screening qualification gate (Stage 1) and live execution on 56 hidden test tasks (Stage 2).

Minimum Requirements

Your entry must pass all four checks to be considered for Stage 1:

1. Submit a Kaggle Writeup (up to 2,000 words) covering all 5 rubric criteria with 3 required figures: (1) an architecture diagram, (2) a score-vs-cost plot, and (3) a dev-set failure breakdown. Un-submitted drafts are not judged.
2. Link your GitHub repository and 40-character commit SHA (git rev-parse HEAD) under Project Links. The repository root must include submission.yaml, serve.py / harness.py, an Apache-2.0 or MIT license, and the unpacked artifacts/ directory. If your repo is private during the competition, install the ple-submission GitHub App and make the repo public at competition close.
3. Set model_api in submission.yaml to one of the 8 official google-cloud/ models when submitting for Stage 2 evaluation (no Google Cloud or Vertex AI billing account is required during local dev; you can run local experiments and generate artifacts/ with any self-hosted open-weight model or personal LLM subscription/API key). In Stage 2, the evaluation proxy blocks custom API keys (.env), external model servers, and web search, and Google supplies the evaluation key at no cost to you.
4. Pass uv run python -m kit check and uv run python -m kit artifacts via the PLE Competition Kit. Committed artifacts/ must be an unpacked directory (at most 512 MiB and 10,000 files, with no Git LFS or symlinks) generated by uv run python eval/run.py.…
detail.data_or_tools:
Dataset & Benchmark Description

In this competition, you will build and evaluate an autonomous agent harness on Physical-Engineering's Last Exam (PLE)—a benchmark of 85 expert-reviewed, long-horizon engineering tasks across four physical engineering disciplines (29 tasks in the public dev set and 56 tasks in the hidden evaluation test set), each running inside an isolated container with a 6-hour time limit.

Unlike static tabular datasets, each PLE task is a full containerized engineering workspace containing up to 50 project files—including multi-sheet PDF construction drawings, 2D/3D CAD and BIM models (IFC4, DXF), load and wire schedules (.xlsx, .csv), geotechnical boring logs, regulatory code excerpts, and local Streamable-HTTP MCP services.

Quick Links & Resources

- PLE Competition Guide & Protocol Spec: https://ple-bench.com/competition/guide
- Instructions for Coding Agents (AGENTS.md): https://ple-bench.com/competition/agents
- Public Dev-Set Task Browser (29 Dev Tasks): https://ple-bench.com/tasks
- PLE Competition Kit & Sample Harnesses (GitHub): https://github.com/google-research/ple
- Starter Submission Template (pi-opus): https://github.com/physical-engineerings-las
detail.submission:
Submit one Kaggle Writeup (not to exceed 2,000 words) before the deadline. You can un-submit, edit, and re-submit until the deadline; un-submitted drafts are not judged.

Your Writeup must include:
1. Coverage of all 5 Stage 1 rubric criteria, a Media Gallery cover image, and 3 figures: (1) an architecture diagram, (2) a score-vs-cost plot, and (3) a failure breakdown on the 29 dev tasks.
2. Your GitHub repo URL under Project Links and 40-character commit SHA (git rev-parse HEAD) at the top of the Writeup. That commit must include submission.yaml (set to one of the 8 google-cloud/* models), serve.py, harness.py, an Apache-2.0 or MIT LICENSE, and the unpacked artifacts/ from uv run python eval/run.py, and pass uv run python -m kit check and uv run python -m kit artifacts. If your repo is private during the competition, install the ple-submission GitHub App and make it public at competition close.
3. If you use an open-weight or custom local judge (JUDGE_MODEL) instead of a frontier model when generating dev scores, you should state which judge model you used in your Writeup.

detail.eligibility:
a. To be eligible to enter the Competition, you must be (i) a registered account holder at Kaggle.com; (ii) the older of 18 years old or the age of majority in your jurisdiction of residence (unless otherwise agreed to by Competition Sponsor and appropriate parental/guardian consents have been obtained by Competition Sponsor); (iii) not a resident of Crimea, so-called Donetsk People's Republic (DNR) or Luhansk People's Republic (LNR), Cuba, Iran, or North Korea; and (iv) not a person or representative of an entity under U.S. export controls or sanctions (see https://ofac.treasury.gov/).

b. Competitions are open to residents of the United States and worldwide, except that if you are a resident of Crimea, so-called Donetsk People's Republic (DNR) or Luhansk People's Republic (LNR), Cuba, Iran, North Korea, or are subject to U.S. export controls or sanctions, you may not enter the Competition. detail.team:
a. The maximum Team (as defined below) size is five (5).

b. Team mergers are allowed and can be performed by the Team leader. In order to merge, the combined Team must have a total Submission count less than or equal to the maximum allowed as of the Team Merger Deadline (as described below). Each team is allowed one Submission; any Submissions submitted by Participants who become part of a Team will be unsubmitted or deleted upon merging.
